contract_plain_english: There is one positive absolute constant c, fixed once and for all, such that: whenever X_1, ..., X_N are independent, mean-zero, sub-exponential random variables and K denotes the largest of their sub-exponential norms max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1} (where ||X||_{psi_1} = inf{ t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2 }), then for every real t >= 0 the probability that the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the average (1/N)(X_1 + ... + X_N) is at least t is at most 2 exp( - c * min(t^2/K^2, t/K) * N ). The prefactor 2 and the factor N are explicit; c is an absolute constant with no numeric value; the factor N multiplies the minimum from outside, and the minimum is taken between the sub-gaussian term t^2/K^2 and the sub-exponential term t/K. Nothing is assumed about boundedness or variances, and the statement is asserted for t = 0 as well.

source_evidence.observation: Rendered page reads: 'Let X_1, ..., X_N be independent, mean zero, sub-exponential random variables. Then, for every t >= 0, we have P{ |(1/N) sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i| >= t } <= 2 exp[ - c min( t^2/K^2 , t/K ) N ] where K = max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}.' The absolute-value bars around the average are present in the rendered page (pdftotext drops them). The factor N sits OUTSIDE the min, multiplying the whole min, still inside the exponent's leading minus sign: '- c min(...) N'.

'In the special case where a_i = 1/N, we obtain a form of Bernstein's inequality for averages:' — so the corollary is Theorem 2.8.2 specialized to the constant weight vector a_i = 1/N, for which ||a||_2^2 = 1/N and ||a||_inf = 1/N.
'This result can be considered as a quantitative form of the law of large numbers for the averages (1/N) sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i.' — interpretive remark only, no additional hypothesis.

'A random variable X that satisfies one of the equivalent properties a-d Proposition 2.7.1 is called a sub-exponential random variable. The sub-exponential norm of X, denoted ||X||_{psi_1}, is defined to be the smallest K_3 in property 3. In other words, ||X||_{psi_1} = inf { t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2 }.' (2.21)
'where c > 0 is an absolute constant.' Corollary 2.8.3 itself does NOT re-declare c; it inherits the book's convention that lower-case c denotes a positive absolute constant.

binders: c: a positive absolute constant, quantified OUTSIDE everything else (existential, chosen once, independent of N, of the random variables, and of t); the statement does not name it in the 'where' clause, inheriting the book's c/C convention
N: the number of summands, appearing as X_1, ..., X_N; implicitly a positive integer (never explicitly bound or constrained in the statement)
X_1, ..., X_N: random variables on a common (unnamed) probability space
t: a real number, universally quantified with 'for every t >= 0'
K: not a free binder but an abbreviation fixed by the trailing clause 'where K = max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}'
conclusions: P{ |(1/N) sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i| >= t } <= 2 exp[ - c min( t^2 / K^2 , t / K ) N ], where K = max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}
The left-hand event is TWO-SIDED: the absolute value of the average exceeds t, with a non-strict inequality '>= t' inside the probability
The right-hand side carries the explicit numeric prefactor 2, the unquantified absolute constant c inside the exponent, and the factor N multiplying the min from outside
definitions_and_conventions: ||X||_{psi_1} (sub-exponential norm) = inf { t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2 } — Definition 2.7.5 / display (2.21), printed page 33
K = max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}, the maximum over i = 1, ..., N of the sub-exponential norms
'sub-exponential random variable' = satisfies one of the equivalent properties a-d of Proposition 2.7.1 (Definition 2.7.5)

Book convention: lower-case c (and upper-case C) denote positive ABSOLUTE constants — not explicit numbers, and not depending on N, the X_i, or t (see 'where c > 0 is an absolute constant', printed page 36)
The average is (1/N) sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i, i.e. the arithmetic mean of the N terms
hypotheses: X_1, ..., X_N are independent (jointly independent; the book says only 'independent')
X_1, ..., X_N are mean zero, i.e. E X_i = 0 for each i
X_1, ..., X_N are sub-exponential random variables in the sense of Definition 2.7.5 (equivalently they satisfy properties a-d of Proposition 2.7.1), so each ||X_i||_{psi_1} is finite
implicit_context: Proposition 2.7.1 (printed pages 31-32) asserts that the parameters K_1, ..., K_5 in its equivalent properties a-e differ from one another by at most an absolute constant factor; footnote 7 makes this precise: there exists an absolute constant C such that property i implies property j with K_j <= C K_i
All random variables are assumed to live on one common probability space; the book states no measurability or integrability hypothesis beyond 'mean zero' and sub-exponentiality
The corollary is derived from Theorem 2.8.2 with a_i = 1/N; the constant c here need not be numerically the same as the c in Theorem 2.8.1 or Theorem 2.8.2, only an absolute constant
Section 2.8 as a whole is announced as 'a concentration inequality for sums of independent sub-exponential random variables' (printed page 36)

details: Two-sided: the event is |average| >= t, so it covers both upper and lower deviations
The prefactor 2 is exactly the price of the two-sidedness (the proof of Theorem 2.8.1 combines the bound for S >= t with the bound for -S >= t)
c is an unquantified positive absolute constant, never given a numeric value
The exponents 2 on t and on K in t^2/K^2 are explicit
N appears as an explicit multiplicative factor outside the min
Exists an absolute constant c > 0 such that: for all N, for all independent mean-zero sub-exponential X_1, ..., X_N, for all t >= 0, the bound holds
c must NOT be allowed to depend on N, on the X_i, or on t
min of a sub-gaussian term t^2/K^2 and a sub-exponential term t/K, the min then scaled by N
Both arguments of the min are normalized by the single scalar K = max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1}, not by a sum of norms
As t -> 0 the bound degenerates to 2, so it is trivially true at t = 0 (the statement still asserts it there)

undebatable_constraints: The probability is of a TWO-SIDED event: absolute value bars around the average (1/N) sum X_i are present in the source
The inequality inside the probability is non-strict: '>= t'
c is an unquantified positive absolute constant (book c/C convention), never an explicit number, and quantified before N, the X_i and t
The factor N multiplies the min from OUTSIDE; it is not inside either argument of the min
The two arguments of the min are exactly t^2/K^2 and t/K, in that order
K is defined as max_i ||X_i||_{psi_1} with ||.||_{psi_1} the sub-exponential norm of Definition 2.7.5, i.e. inf{ t > 0 : E exp(|X|/t) <= 2 }
Hypotheses are exactly: independent, mean zero, sub-exponential; no boundedness and no variance hypothesis
The bound is asserted for every t >= 0, t = 0 included
The sum is normalized by 1/N (an average), not an unnormalized sum and not a 1/sqrt(N) normalization
